info.name: AI Pipeline on Restate — core-api
info.description:
The complete core-api surface: health, the catalogue, trigger management, starting and inspecting runs, the run lifecycle, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and the control plane.

**Setup**
1. Select the `Local` environment (or edit the collection variables).
2. Bring the stack up: `docker compose up -d --build`.
3. Deploy the example units: `pnpm pipeline deploy summary && pnpm pipeline deploy content-enrichment`.
4. For the RAG folder: `pnpm pipeline deploy rag-query && pnpm pipeline deploy rag-ingest`.

**How the variables work**
`Start a run` and `List runs` save `runId` into a collection variable, so the run requests below them work without copy-pasting. Same for `deploymentId` from `List deployments`. And for `ragRunId` from 'Add or replace documents'.

**Errors** all use one envelope: `{ "error": { "code", "message" } }`. The codes are a closed set — see `packages/api-contract/src/errors.ts`.

**Not in here:** the Restate admin API (`:9070`) and the Restate ingress (`:8080`). The ingress is deliberately not published; REST goes through this API.

item.name: Triggers
item.description: Enabling and disabling a unit's triggers. Disabling a Kafka trigger is eventually consistent, and the response says so.

request.description:
Sets the desired state and reconciles Restate's subscriptions.

Deleting a subscription stops its consumer group, but records Restate has already enqueued still start runs — so `observedStatus` reads `disabling` until the subscription is gone, and `disabled` never means 'nothing in flight'. The response carries a `note` saying exactly that.

Re-enabling reuses a stable `group.id`, so the consumer resumes from its committed offsets rather than replaying the topic.

item.name: Runs
item.description: Starting runs and reading them back. Restate is the run store — there is no run table — so these views are assembled from Restate's introspection plus the state each handler records at its start.

header.description: Optional. The run id is derived from it, so the same key returns the same run.

request.description:
202 with `{ runId, invocationId, status }` and a `Location` header.

`status` is `Accepted`, or `PreviouslyAccepted` when an `Idempotency-Key` matched a run that already exists. Note the semantics: the run id is derived from the key, so **the same key with different input returns the first run and ignores the new input**.

The body carries only the input. The trigger context is attached by the control plane, so a caller cannot claim a run came from somewhere it did not.

Refusals: `NOT_INVOCABLE` (not a public workflow), `NO_REST_TRIGGER`, `TRIGGER_DISABLED`, `NOT_DEPLOYED`, `INVALID_INPUT`. They are checked in that order, so the most useful one wins.

item.name: Run lifecycle
item.description: Operator actions on a run in flight. Cancel asks the handler to unwind; kill does not; resume revives a run whose retries were exhausted.

request.description:
202 `cancellation_requested`. Graceful: the handler gets to unwind, so compensation runs.

409 `RUN_COMPLETED` if it has already finished.

exec: pm.test('202 requested, or 409 if it already finished', () => {

request.description: 202 `kill_requested`. Unlike cancel, the handler does not unwind: no compensation runs and children are abandoned. For a run that cancel cannot stop.

exec: pm.test('202 requested, or 409 if it already finished', () => {

request.description:
202 `resume_requested`.

The counterpart to a deliberate design choice: the LLM retry profile is uncapped, so a gateway outage leaves work retrying rather than failing it — an outage should not destroy a run's journal.

**Usually the thing that needs resuming is not the run.** A workflow waiting on a stuck service call is only suspended, so it reads `running`. `GET /v1/runs/{workflow}/{runId}` lists those calls in `blocked`, with the invocation id, the target and the last failure. Send that id as `invocationId` to resume the call itself; omit the body to resume the run's own invocation.

Only a `paused` call is resumable — one that is `backing-off` is still retrying and needs the cause fixed, not a resume.

409 `RUN_NOT_RESUMABLE` if the target is running or has completed. 404 if `invocationId` is not a call of this run.

exec: pm.test('202 requested, or 409 if it is not paused', () => {

item.name: RAG
item.description:
Retrieval-augmented generation over collections of documents.

Reads, searches and answers are calls to the `rag-query` service through Restate. Adding, deleting and dropping start `rag-ingest` runs, answered 202 with a run to follow, as any run start is.

core-api routes these requests without interpreting them: it checks the path, the query string and that a body is a JSON object (at most 64 levels deep; 64 KiB for a search or an answer), and the units validate the rest. A DELETE takes no body. Their answers are passed through as they are, and their refusals keep their own messages.

**Setup:** `pnpm pipeline deploy rag-query && pnpm pipeline deploy rag-ingest`. Until then these requests answer 409 `NOT_DEPLOYED`.

**Errors from `rag-query`:** 400 `INVALID_INPUT` (it rejected the request), 404 `NOT_FOUND` (no such collection or document), 502 `RESTATE_INGRESS_ERROR` (it failed, or was canceled or killed), 503 `RESTATE_UNAVAILABLE` (Restate is overloaded or unreachable), and 504 `RESTATE_UNAVAILABLE` when it does not answer in time: `RAG_QUERY_TIMEOUT_MS` (30 s) for reads and searches, `RAG_ANSWER_TIMEOUT_MS` (240 s) for answers and for searches that rerank.

**In a collection run** 'Follow the ingest run' repeats until the run has finished, so the requests after it find the document. Sent on its own, it shows the run as it stands.

header.description: Optional. The run id is derived from it, so the same key returns the same run.

request.description:
Starts a `rag-ingest` run that chunks, embeds and stores each document. The collection is created on first use, and `collectionSettings` (embedding model, index) apply only then.

The body is the run's input without `operation` and `collection`, which come from the route and the path: `documents` (each `{ id, text, format?, title?, metadata?, version? }`), and optionally `options` and `collectionSettings`.

202 with `{ runId, invocationId, status }` and a `Location`. The run's `output` says how each document fared — see 'Follow the ingest run'. `Idempotency-Key` works as it does for 'Start a run'.

Refusals: `NOT_DEPLOYED` (rag-ingest), `INVALID_REQUEST` (no `documents`), `INVALID_INPUT` (rag-ingest's catalogued schema rejected the input; the message lists the failing paths).

exec: pm.test('202 with the rag-ingest run that stores them', () => {

request.description:
The run 'Add or replace documents' started, read like any other run. Once it has `completed`, its `output` reports each document as `written`, `unchanged`, `superseded` (a newer version is already stored), `deleted`, `absent` or `failed`, with the reason.

Ingestion is asynchronous. In a collection run this request repeats, 2 s apart and at most 60 times, until the run has finished, then checks that the document was stored; the requests after it rely on that. Sent on its own, it shows the run as it stands.

request.description:
Semantic search: the query is embedded with the collection's query template and matched against its chunks, best first.

Body: `query`, and optionally `topK`, a `filter` on chunk metadata, `minScore`, `includeVector` and `rerank`. The collection comes from the path; one in the body is ignored.

A search with a `rerank` object waits as long as an answer (`RAG_ANSWER_TIMEOUT_MS`), and `Idempotency-Key` works for it as it does for an answer.

header.description: Optional. A retry of the same question with the same key gets the same answer.

request.description:
Retrieves evidence as 'Search' does, then has an LLM answer from it, citing its sources as `[S1]`, `[S2]`… When the evidence does not support an answer, the response says so instead of guessing.

Body: `question`, the search fields, and optionally `model`, `temperature`, `maxOutputTokens`, `maxContextChars` and `instructions`.

This waits on an LLM: up to `RAG_ANSWER_TIMEOUT_MS` (240 s by default), then 504. With an `Idempotency-Key`, a retry of the same question gets the answer Restate already holds instead of a second LLM call. The key is bound to the question, so reusing it for a different one asks afresh rather than returning a stale answer.

item.name: Control plane
item.description: Deployment registration and retirement. `pnpm pipeline deploy` is what normally calls these — it builds the image and starts the container first, which this collection cannot do.

request.description:
Every deployment with its `inFlight` count — invocations still pinned to it, which must finish there before it can be retired.

`status` mirrors Restate's routing rather than leading it: the deployment Restate sends new invocations to is `active`, every other live one is `draining`.

exec: // Prefer one that is actually retirable. Failing that, take a live one so the retire request
// below demonstrates the refusal rather than an id-validation error.

request.description:
**Use `pnpm pipeline deploy <unit>` instead.** This request is here to document the shape; sent as-is it fails, because no container serves that endpoint.

The order of operations matters. Everything that can be refused cheaply is refused first, while nothing has changed; then the endpoint is discovered with `dry_run` to check what it serves; only then is it registered with Restate. After that every step is idempotent, so a failure comes back as a retryable 503 rather than being rolled back — by then Restate may already be routing to the endpoint.

Pre-registration refusals (safe for the CLI to tear the container down again): `INVALID_METADATA`, `INVALID_SCHEMA`, `INVALID_CONFIG`, `RESTATE_NAME_TAKEN`, `VERSION_CONTRACT_CONFLICT`, `VERSION_ARTIFACT_CONFLICT`, `DEPENDENCY_NOT_REGISTERED`, `DEPENDENCY_NOT_DEPLOYED`, `SERVICE_MISMATCH`.

A version binds to one contract and one artifact: the same `name@version` from different bytes is a 409.

Refused in three cases, in order of how badly getting it wrong would hurt: the catalogue marks it `active`; Restate still routes to it (which wins over the catalogue if they disagree); or invocations are still pinned to it.

`DEPLOYMENT_ACTIVE` or `DEPLOYMENT_NOT_DRAINED`. Idempotent once retired.

This removes the Restate deployment but not the container — `pnpm pipeline retire <id>` does both.

exec: pm.test('retires a drained deployment, or explains why not', () => {
// DEPLOYMENT_ACTIVE and DEPLOYMENT_NOT_DRAINED are the interesting ones: both mean Restate
// still needs this deployment, which is exactly what this endpoint exists to protect.

item.name: Guards
item.description: There is no auth in v1. Every port binds to 127.0.0.1, and two guards carry the weight.

request.description:
A Host allow-list is what stops DNS rebinding — a page on the public internet resolving a name it controls to 127.0.0.1 and talking to this API from the victim's browser.

Postman may not let you override `Host`; if it does not, this returns 200 and the guard is untested here. `apps/core-api/src/app.test.ts` covers it.

Unsafe methods carrying a foreign `Origin`, or `sec-fetch-site: cross-site|same-site`, are refused — so a foreign page cannot make a browser start or cancel runs. The CLI and curl send neither header, so they are unaffected.
Even a 404 uses the error envelope, so a client never has to parse two failure shapes.
